title: A way of escape (1 Corinthians 10)
hook: no temptation beyond what you can bear, and the way out comes with it
tomorrow: what happens when a church dinner splits into full and hungry?

segments.voice: Yesterday Paul ran: all things to all people, every habit bent, one steady course. So run. Today, what pulls a runner off the track.
screen: `SO RUN.` → `WHAT PULLS YOU OFF THE TRACK?`

segments.voice: Midnight. A reply typed out, thumb over send, and you already know you'll regret it. Here's an odd detail in what Paul says about moments like that. He promises a way out, and then he says when it shows up: "with the temptation." Not after the feeling passes, not once you've calmed down. With it. Why would the exit come packed inside the trap?
screen: `THUMB OVER SEND.` → `A WAY OUT, WITH THE TEMPTATION.` → `WHY THERE?`

segments.voice: First the warning. Paul retells Israel's wilderness years as family history, "all our fathers," and says those things "are written for our admonition." Then, to a church that feels very secure: "Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall." Then the comfort, in one long sentence: "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it." Three promises in it. You're not the first; it's common to man. It won't be beyond what you're able. And there's a door. Now the puzzle. The door comes with the temptation because that's when it's needed; an exit that waited until the pull was gone would help nobody. And look at what it's for: "that ye may be able to bear it." Some readers hear a way through, as much as a way out. Then Paul shows a door in use: "Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry." Flee. Sometimes the exit is plain: stand up, leave the room. One to tell a friend tonight: the popular saying is that God never gives you more than you can handle. Paul's line is narrower. It's about temptation, and what it promises is a door.
screen: `TAKE HEED LEST HE FALL.` · `COMMON TO MAN.` · `THE DOOR COMES WITH IT.` · `FLEE: LEAVE THE ROOM.` · then, large: `A WAY TO ESCAPE.`

segments.voice: Look at the nearest door, or picture one. Bring to mind one pull that keeps coming back, a screen, a habit, a sharp tongue, and find its door: the moment it starts, and the small move that walks you out, like standing up or one slow breath before you answer. If you pray, you can rest on Paul's four words: God is faithful.
A way of escape. Paul's promise that alongside the temptation God makes a door, so it can be borne.
The line to keep: a way to escape, built right into the moment you need it. Day done.

notes: Israel's wilderness story is told as Paul tells it, as 'our fathers', and is not set up as a foil. 10:1–10 is summarized only as 'wilderness years'.
Puzzle: 'the door comes with the temptation because that's when it's needed' is an explanation of 10:13's 'with the temptation', not a quotation. 'Some readers hear a way through' is hedged. Confirm.
The popular saying 'God never gives you more than you can handle' is contrasted with 10:13 (myth item and teach); a pastoral reviewer may want to check the tone.
